result: The authors developed HIV-AFMACS, an HIV reporter virus encoding a streptavidin-binding affinity tag (SBP-ΔLNGFR) at the cell surface, enabling antibody-free magnetic cell sorting. The optimal construct (pNL4-3-ΔEnv-Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR) expressed high levels of LNGFR early in infection (24 hr) in both CEM-T4s and primary CD4+ T cells, and routinely achieved ≥90% purity with ≤10% loss of infected cells.
evaluation: Claims C1-C38 collectively demonstrate successful development and validation of the HIV-AFMACS system. The design strategy (C25-C27), construct selection based on expression kinetics (C28-C35), and performance metrics (C36-C37) are well-documented with experimental data and figures. The system addresses key methodological requirements for studying HIV infection in primary cells.

result: Time course proteomic analysis of HIV-infected primary CD4+ T cells quantitated 9070 cellular proteins across 10 conditions, revealing extensive T cell activation-dependent remodeling (29% of proteins changing >2-fold) and HIV-specific regulation of known accessory protein targets including tetherin (Vpu), SAMHD1 (not targeted by HIV-1), and substrates of Vif, Nef, Vpu, and Vpr.
evaluation: Claims C3-C50 describe comprehensive time course proteomic data with appropriate controls for T cell activation. The quantitation of ~9000 proteins (C4, C39) and validation of known targets (C41-C47) with proper citations demonstrate technical rigor. Temporal expression patterns of viral proteins (C49-C50) are consistent with HIV biology.

result: Single time point proteomic analysis across three donors identified 650 HIV-dependent changes (q<0.05) in 8789 quantitated proteins, with 46% (297/650) attributable to known accessory protein effects. Downregulated pathways included DNA damage response/cell cycle (Vpr), cytidine deamination/PP2A activity (Vif), and amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef), while upregulated pathways included lipid and sterol metabolism.
evaluation: Claims C5, C51-C62 provide reproducible findings across multiple donors with appropriate statistical thresholds (q<0.05). The pathway analysis (C57-C62) is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment and consistent with prior literature. The quantitative breakdown of accessory protein contributions (C56) demonstrates systematic analysis.

result: 192 proteins (30% of HIV-regulated proteins) were either not detected or not significantly regulated in CEM-T4 cells, including ARID5A and PTPN22. These proteins were validated by immunoblot and, based on temporal regulation patterns, identified as likely novel Vpr substrates specific to primary T cells.
evaluation: Claims C63-C64, C7-C8, C69-C71, C77-C78 identify primary T cell-specific targets with multiple lines of evidence: proteomic detection (C69), quantitative depletion (C70), immunoblot validation (C71), and temporal profiling consistent with Vpr activity (C77). The inference about Vpr dependence (C77) is supported by comparison with known Vpr substrate ARID5B (C78).

result: DPH7 and FMR1 were identified as novel Vif-dependent targets. Both APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins were depleted in WT but not ΔVif virus-infected cells. Vif-dependent depletion of PPP2R5D was confirmed by immunoblot with functional validation through increased AURKB phosphorylation. DPH7 and FMR1 depletion was validated in both viral infection and single transgene expression systems, demonstrating Vif is necessary and sufficient for their degradation.
evaluation: Claims C6, C79-C91 provide comprehensive validation of novel Vif targets through multiple experimental approaches: comparative proteomics (WT vs ΔVif), immunoblot validation (C83, C88, C89), functional readout (C84), and necessity/sufficiency testing (C89-C90). The claim that these targets account for all significant Vif-dependent changes (C91) is well-supported by the systematic analysis.

result: Control experiments with lentivectors expressing SBP-ΔLNGFR alone or with Tat showed minimal perturbation (37/8518 proteins, 0.4%) and only 1/650 HIV-regulated proteins (MYB) was also regulated by control vectors. No Tat-dependent changes were detected despite robust LTR transactivation.
evaluation: Claims C65-C68 provide critical negative controls demonstrating that the AFMACS system itself does not cause artifactual changes. The quantitative assessment (C66, C68) and lack of Tat effects (C67) despite functional transactivation strengthen confidence that observed changes are HIV-specific.

result: Temporal profiling distinguished Vpr substrates (near-maximal depletion by 24 hr in infected and partially in uninfected cells due to virion-packaged Vpr) from Vif/Nef/Vpu substrates (progressive depletion from 24-48 hr only in infected cells requiring de novo synthesis).
evaluation: Claims C72-C76 demonstrate that temporal patterns can distinguish accessory protein mechanisms. The mechanistic explanation for Vpr effects (C73-C74, virion packaging) is supported by appropriate citations, and the observed patterns (C75-C76) are consistent with known HIV biology.

result: This study generated the first high-coverage proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells. Primary T cell-specific proteins were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV than proteins detected in both cell types (10.5% vs 6.9%, p<0.0001). The depth of coverage (>90% proteins quantitated by ≥2 peptides) and high purity (>90% infected) maximized signal-to-noise ratio.
evaluation: Claims C95-C97, C103-C106 establish the novelty and quality of the resource. The statistical comparison (C97) demonstrates biological significance of using primary cells. Technical metrics (C104-C106) support data quality claims, though the assertion of being 'first high coverage' (C95) should be qualified given the Kuo et al. 2018 study.

result: Comparison with a recent study (Kuo et al. 2018) that quantitated 7761 proteins at 96 hr post-infection showed that 413/650 (64%) of HIV-dependent changes identified in this study were obscured in that dataset, including depletion of ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7 and 19/51 known accessory protein substrates.
evaluation: Claims C100-C102 provide quantitative comparison with prior work, demonstrating advantages of the current approach. The specific enumeration of missed targets (C102) supports the claim of superior sensitivity, though the comparison is complicated by different time points (48 hr vs 96 hr) and viral constructs.

result: VSVg pseudotyping was used to enhance titers and enable synchronous infections, but may redirect viral entry and abrogate Env-dependent signaling. Only 1/650 HIV-dependent changes was observed in control lentivector-transduced cells, suggesting minimal false positives, though false negatives from absent Env-CD4 interactions remain possible.
evaluation: Claims C107-C110 acknowledge important methodological limitations. The quantitative assessment of false positives (C109) is rigorous, while the discussion of potential false negatives (C110) appropriately qualifies the findings. The rationale for VSVg use (C107) is sound given the experimental goals.

result: The introduction establishes that viral infection causes host proteome remodeling through direct viral effects, secondary effects, or host countermeasures, which can be differentiated by temporal profiling. Primary T cells are superior to transformed cell lines (like CEM-T4) because accessory proteins Vif, Nef, and Vpu are required in primary but not many transformed T cells, and high MOI experiments may not reflect single provirus effects.
evaluation: Claims C9-C18 provide appropriate background and rationale from cited literature. The limitations of cell lines (C15-C17) and high MOI approaches (C18) justify the experimental design. These are well-established concepts in the field supported by appropriate citations.

result: AFMACS-based selection offers advantages over conventional methods: it is faster, simpler, and more scalable than FACS, and avoids artifacts from antibody-mediated receptor cross-linking or bead internalization because cells are released with biotin.
evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe methodological advantages supported by appropriate citations. These are comparative statements about technique rather than novel findings, but provide important context for why AFMACS was chosen.

result: Temporal profiling is well-suited for identifying direct viral targets, and accessory proteins account for most proteomic remodeling in HIV-infected cells. Downregulated proteins correlate well between primary T cells and cell lines due to abundant direct accessory protein targets, while upregulated proteins show less concordance, possibly reflecting indirect, cell-type-specific transcriptional effects.
evaluation: Claims C111-C115 provide interpretive synthesis of the results. The distinction between downregulated (direct) and upregulated (indirect) changes (C113-C115) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the mechanistic explanation for upregulated proteins (C115) remains somewhat speculative.

result: Novel HIV targets identified in this study (FMR1, ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7) impact processes relevant for HIV replication including virus infectivity, inflammatory signaling, T cell activation, and translational fidelity, underscoring the value of unbiased systems-level approaches.
evaluation: Claims C116-C121 place findings in functional context using appropriate citations. While the specific roles of these proteins in HIV infection require further investigation, their known functions (C117-C120) in relevant processes are well-documented. The concluding statement (C121) appropriately emphasizes the discovery aspect.

result: Some reported Vpu/Nef substrates may be downregulated from the plasma membrane without protein degradation (e.g., NTB-A, CCR7) or may have expression prevented without reduction below baseline (e.g., ICAM-1/3), explaining why not all reported targets were detected in this proteomic analysis.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 provide reasonable explanations for discrepancies with prior literature, supported by appropriate citations. This acknowledges that whole-cell proteomics may miss membrane redistribution or prevention of upregulation, which are valid limitations of the approach.
